**(p-85) Surat al-Layl (The Night): its purpose**

Its purpose is to point to the purpose of Surat al-Shams (The Sun), which is the complete disposal of souls. This is shown by establishing the perfection of power through choice, with people differing in their striving while their aims are united, and in their desire to reach the refuge (al-malādh) of the pleasures of the belly and the private parts and the comfort that follows from them. Its name is al-Layl (The Night). Its clearest indication of this lies in reflecting on the oath and its answer, and in reaching what is correct from that. Also, the night itself points to this, because it runs contrary to the soul's desire through what it contains of darkness and sleep, which is the brother of death. This [prevents] most desires and requires most opposites.

*In the name of God, who has manifest greatness and dazzling wisdom,*
*the Merciful, whose blessing encompassed His origination of things and His clarification of them, in successive waves;*
*the Compassionate, who singled out whoever wills Him with what pleases Him, so He made him one who praises and thanks Him.*

* *

Since (the Surah of al-Shams) explained the condition of the one who purified his soul and the condition of the one who corrupted it, and clarified, at its end, (p-86) the opposition of Thamud to their Messenger and what destroyed them, he (the author) knew that people differ in their striving to obtain the highland of good and the highland of evil. Some of them are overcome by the darkness of confusion, and others are overcome by the daylight of guidance. Thus they differ in their aims, their sources, and their destinations. After establishing that He is the One who disposes souls toward wickedness and piety, He swore at the beginning of this (Surah) by what indicates the wonders of His making in harm and benefit, as a reminder of the completeness of His power, in that He is the Agent by choice. He comes between a person and his heart until He brings him to pursue his aim, not by the opposite of what leads to it, but by what leads to its opposite. [And] it is because He hardly lets anyone affirm unity of aim while differing in striving and in attainment. He also explained the recompense of each, as a warning against the highland of evil and an encouragement toward the highland of good, and He clarified what purifies and what corrupts. So He said:

﴿By the night﴾, i.e., the night which is the sign of darkness, the cause of confusion and mixing up of what it brings about of perplexity and obscurity in conditions and in the (new) moons that lead to the darkness of nonexistence. It is the place of secrets, by what it brings to the righteous and cuts off from the wicked.

﴿When it covers﴾, i.e., it veils what existed visible in the light of day gradually, little by little, and what it indicates of the majesty of its Originator and the greatness of its erasing and its rising (p-87).

"By the day when it becomes manifest" — [meaning] the day which is the cause of the unveiling of matters, like death, which removes from the soul the attachments of the body, so that there becomes clear to it what it was in of ugly deeds; and [like] the openness (al-jahr) which expands the self by removing confusion. ﴿When it becomes manifest﴾, i.e., appears with a great appearing by the light of the sun, and reveals what was hidden, leaving no confusion for any beholder. Whoever desires secrecy aims for the night, and whoever desires openness aims for the day, whether he is of the righteous or of the wicked.

Al-Biqa'i, Nazm al-Durar, on surah 92, verse 3:

When he (al-Biqa'i) mentioned the ones who are mixed in meaning (al-mutakhalitin ma'nan), he followed them with those who are mixed in the senses (al-mutakhalitin hissan), and he said, explicitly stating in them what was intended in the first, and he singled out this one for explicit mention as an alert that he, being rational, may err in himself, so he claims divinity or incarnation (al-ittihad), or other forms of atheism (al-ilhad): ﴿And He who created﴾. The rule of expression with "ma" (what), whose predominant use is for non-rational beings, has been mentioned in surah al-Shams, as a warning to them that when they associated with Him, glorified and exalted is He, what does not reason, they gave it that station, though He has encompassed all things, and He is the One who created the scholars, while they cannot encompass Him in knowledge. [Mentioned together with] what "ma" conveys of amazement at them in that matter, since it is the form of amazement.

﴿The male﴾: in the senses, by the instrument of the man, and in meaning, by resolve and strength. ﴿And the female﴾: in the senses, by the instrument of the woman, and in meaning, by lowliness of resolve and weakness of strength. What they both indicate of great craftsmanship, dazzling invention and origination is that His distinction between them, though both are from one matter, which is dust, indicates the completeness of His power, which entails the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and of His deliberate action. So the verse is of the type of ihtibak: it mentions first the craftsmanship, indicating its omission second, and second the craftsman, indicating its omission first.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 92, verse 4:

When he had mentioned what is perceptibly contrary among meanings and bodies, he followed it with what is intellectually contrary among accidents, and said: ﴿Indeed, your striving﴾, that is, your work, O people charged with obligation, in reaching one single goal. For this reason he emphasized it, because the diversity of the ways of striving hardly accords with the unity of the aim. He expressed it as "striving" so that each person would exert the utmost of his effort in his work. ﴿Is diverse﴾, that is, differs with extreme difference according to the difference already mentioned. It is a plural of shatit, like قَتْلى (qatla, "slain") and قَتِيلٍ (qatil, "a slain one"). So a human being is a man in aspiration and a woman in resolve, and a woman in aspiration and a man in action. Thus you oppose one another in beliefs, you contend with one another in doctrines, and you differ to the utmost degree of difference in good and bad deeds: one strives to free his soul, and another strives to destroy it. Hence it is known with certainty that there must be one who is right and one who is wrong, and one who pleases God and one who angers Him, because it is not permissible for two opposites to be united in the attribute of pleasing or angering. Thus what the polytheists intended by their saying, ﴿If God had willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him﴾ [al-Nahl: 35] [the verse], and what resembles it, is refuted.

Al-Imam Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Zubayr said: When He had previously explained their state of divergence, He swore by that matter among creatures, according to His decree from eternity, "that He may test them, which of them is best in deed." So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, your striving is diverse﴾, which connects to His saying: ﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ [al-Shams: 9] ﴿and he has failed who corrupts it﴾ [al-Shams: 10]. His saying, ﴿As for he who gives and fears God﴾ [al-Layl: 5] up to ﴿for the difficult﴾ [al-Layl: 10], is consistent with it in explanation and reminder of the matter as it stands: that good and evil are by His will and inspiration, and according to what precedes. His saying ﴿and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾ [al-Shams: 8] is also of this kind. He, exalted is He, is the one who inspires toward giving, fearing God, and almsgiving, and who decrees stinginess, self-sufficiency, and denial. ﴿And God created you and what you do﴾ [al-Saffat: 96]. ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23]. Then he increased this clarification by His saying: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is guidance﴾ [al-Layl: 12] ﴿and indeed, to Us belong the Hereafter and the first﴾ [al-Layl: 13]. So woe to the Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination) and the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school that denied the eternal divine decree in human acts): ﴿And how many a sign in the heavens and the earth they pass by, while they turn away from it﴾ [Yusuf: 105]. Ended.

When he matched the oath with what is sworn to, and alerted, through the oath and the emphasis together with the clear presence of what is sworn to, that they are secure in their security while being warned, like one who claims there is no difference and that the outcome of all is one, as the proponents of *al-Wahda* (the doctrine of the unity of existence) say, may they be disgraced and cursed, he began an explanation of the scattering of their efforts and an explanation of the recompense for them. So he said, as a consequence of their divergence (p-90), stating what is fixed in natural dispositions: that it is not permissible to equate the doer of good with the doer of evil. He displayed for the one who purified his soul, or corrupted it, a clear display, indicating that the obedient among this community, praise be to Allah, are many, as good tidings for its Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿As for he who gives﴾, i.e., giving occurred from him according to what We have specified for him and commanded him with, ﴿and fears [Allah]﴾, i.e., *taqwa* (God-consciousness, piety) occurred from him, which is taking up protections through acts of obedience and avoiding sins, out of fear of Our punishments.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 92, verse 6:

﴿And affirmed﴾, i.e., he brought about the affirmation of what was reported, ﴿the best﴾, i.e., which is the word of justice (kalimat al-adl), which is the best of speech, namely (the affirmation of) tawhid (divine oneness) and what branches out from it of true promises concerning the Hereafter, and the replacing (of what is spent) in the provision of this world, and the manifestation of the religion even though its adherents are few, "upon the whole religion" (cf. Qur'an 9:33), and other than that, of everything the Messenger (ﷺ) was promised by Him, glorified and exalted be He. The discourse shifted to the locus of majesty (maẓhar al-‘aẓama) as an indication of the difficulty of obedience for the self, even though it is in itself at the utmost ease, because it is at the utmost burden upon the self. So He said:

﴿So We will ease him﴾: that is, We will prepare him with what We possess of greatness, by a promise in which there is no breaking. ﴿for ease﴾: that is, the disposition that is in the utmost ease and comfort, from the mercy that requires acting in what pleases Him, glory be to Him and exalted, so that he reaches what He is pleased with of (p-٩١) the good life and entering the Garden.

When al-Biqa'i had mentioned the one who purifies himself (al-muzakki) and its fruit, he followed it with the one who corrupts himself (al-mudassi) and his wretchedness, saying: ﴿But as for he who is stingy﴾, i.e., who brought this wicked reality into being, withholding what He commanded and urged him to do, ﴿and considers himself self-sufficient﴾, i.e., who sought self-sufficiency from people and from what He promised of reward, and who made himself so through what his deficient self and his false assumptions suggested to him. Thus he did not do good to people, nor did he work for the Hereafter.
﴿And denied﴾, i.e., he brought about denial of what deserves to be affirmed, ﴿the best﴾, i.e., he rejected it. And since he was fixed upon sensible things like the beasts, he said:

﴿So We will ease him toward ﴾ — that is, We shall prepare him, by Our grandeur, a promise that will not fail — ﴿toward hardship﴾, that is, toward the trait that is the most difficult and wretched of things, namely acting in a way that angers Him, glorified is He, which necessitates entry into the Fire and what leads to it. By his use of the plural "We" (nūn al-ʿaẓama, the "nūn of majesty") in both "the path of good" (najd al-khayr) and "the path of evil" (najd al-sharr), he indicates that a person's committing either of them is at the furthest extreme: as for the path of good, it is because it is surrounded by hardships; as for the path of evil, it is because of the restraints against it found in reason and in the primordial nature (al-fiṭra al-ūlā). All of this is a matter that has already been settled in eternity, through the determination of who are the people of felicity and who are the people of wretchedness. [«And each one, as the Prophet ﷺ said, is made easy for that for which he was created».

Since people of this world, when they fall into a predicament, rescue themselves from it with their wealth, He said: ﴿And his wealth will not avail him﴾, i.e., in that situation, ﴿him﴾, i.e., this one who was stingy and denied, ﴿his wealth﴾, i.e., that which he withheld, hoping for its benefit. It is also permissible that this be an interrogative of denial, in which case it negates any benefit in the most emphatic manner: ﴿when he falls (taradda)﴾, i.e., perishes by plunging into the pit of the grave. And "taradda" is on the pattern of "tafa'ala" from al-radaa (ruin, destruction), which is perdition and falling into a well.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 92, verse 12:

When it might be said by the captious ignoramus, who is unaware of the majesty of Him, glory be to Him and exalted, against which no one has any objection, "Why does He not make everything easy for the good (al-husna)?", He resumed His answer, making clear what He obligated Himself to of benefits out of His bounty, through His subtlety and generosity, and what He does of things that are His own, without regard for that, by virtue of His might and greatness. So He said, emphasizing, as an alert that He loves the knowledge that no one has any right over Him at all: ﴿Indeed, upon Us﴾, that is, upon what We have of majesty, ﴿is the guidance﴾, that is, the making clear of the path of truth and the establishment of clear proofs for it.

When He explained what He had bound Himself to, His Most Holy self, so that it became as though it were incumbent upon Him because its occurrence was certain, it might have given the impression that something was obligatory for Him. So He followed it with what negates that and indicates that He has complete disposal (*tasarruf*, full control over affairs), so that nothing He wills is difficult for Him. He said: ﴿Indeed, to Us belong the Hereafter and the first [life].﴾ That is, O deniers, (it belongs) specifically to Us. He placed first what is more important to them, because of their denial, and not for the sake of the verse-ending (*fāṣila*, the rhyming final word of a verse). For it would have served the verse-ending equally well to say: "for the immediate and the other," so He said: ﴿for the Hereafter and the first.﴾ (p-93) Whoever abandons what We have made clear to him of the path of guidance does not thereby cease to belong to Us, and he harms only himself. And to Us belongs complete disposal, by means of the causes We establish that bring a thing very near, and then by means of the obstacles We establish that cause it to be extremely far. So We give whom We will what We will, and We withhold from whom We will what We will. Whoever seeks either of these from other than Us, his opinion is void and his effort is lost. The placement (of words) is not for the sake of the verse-ending, for the invalidity of this has been established, and it is not permissible to hold this view in more than one place, among them the end of Surat Bara'a. There is no difference between one who believes that in it there is something measured merely for the sake of metre so that it becomes poetry (*shi'r*), and one who believes that in it [something] has been put forward or put back merely for the sake of the verse-ending so that it becomes rhymed prose (*saj'*). Moreover, if [this] were only for the sake of the verse-ending, it would be possible to say: "for the first and the other," or "for the former and the other," for example.

When Glorified and Exalted is He had informed that He has made the Sacred Exposition (al-bayan) binding upon Himself, and that to Him belongs everything, which necessarily entails the comprehensiveness of knowledge and the all-encompassing scope of power, He explained this by what He made a consequence of it, turning the speech away from the pronoun to the manifestation of majesty (mazhar al-'azamah), for the sake of tenderness toward the addressees, in order to dispel illusion and bring understanding near. So He said: ﴿Then I have warned you﴾, that is, I have cautioned you, O you who oppose the path I have made clear, ﴿of a Fire that blazes﴾, that is, one that kindles and flares up with a flaring that is at the utmost intensity, without any effort in it upon its kindler at all (p-94), nor any of its keepers, by what the dropping of the ta' indicates, and in the assimilation (idgham) there is also an indication that the least of the Fire of the Hereafter is likewise, so that warning of what blazes and of what is above that becomes a matter of a fortiori reasoning (min bab al-awla).

Since it has already been mentioned more than once that each of the doer of good and the doer of evil is singled out for his own abode by way of restriction (ḥaṣr), in denial that a doer of good should be made equal to a doer of evil in anything, and since restriction by "lā" (not) and "illā" (except) is the clearest of its types, He said: ﴿None shall enter it﴾, meaning, shall endure its heat and its intensity by way of being constantly bound to it and immersed in it, ﴿except the most wretched﴾, meaning the one who is at the peak of wretchedness, and that is the disbeliever. For the wicked person, even if he enters it, it does not happen to him by way of constancy (luzūm), and for this reason He described him with His saying, exalted is He:
﴿Who denied﴾: that is, he corrupted his cognitive faculty by turning away from the truth out of arrogance and obstinacy, so he did not give his wealth for the purification of his soul.

{"Translation"}

**﴿And he will be spared it﴾**, i.e., the Fire described with a promise that admits no breach, will be near, with what the sīn (the prefix of future tense) conveys of emphasis together with deferment, and his being spared it with the utmost ease, with what the passive construction conveys. **﴿The most fearing (al-Atqā)﴾**, i.e., the one who founded his scholarly strength in the most thorough manner possible, so he was at the summit of the rank of taqwā (God-consciousness). He is the one who guarded himself against shirk (associating partners with God) and sins, and it is understood from this that whoever is not at the summit [of taqwā] is not like this, for the wrongdoer (fāsiq) enters it and then comes out of it, and this does not contradict the earlier restriction.

Having mentioned what pertains to the cognitive faculty (al-quwwa al-'ilmiyya), he followed it with what concerns the practical faculty (al-quwwa al-'amaliyya), saying: ﴿He who gives his wealth﴾, i.e., he spends it in the channels of goodness. For this reason he explained it with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that he may purify himself﴾, i.e., he cleanses himself of filth and defilements by purifying his soul and causing it to grow through that giving, by distancing himself from bad character traits and adhering to their good qualities, because he did not deny and did not turn away. The verse is of the type of ihtibak (interlocking ellipsis): He mentioned denial first as an indication of the omission of its opposite second, and the giving of wealth second as an indication of the omission of its opposite first.

Since a person may give in order to purify himself, by repaying a debt of gratitude and rewarding favors, He said: ﴿And not for anyone has he any favor [that] is recompensed﴾, meaning, while the situation is that there is nothing owed to anyone from him; and he intensified the negation, so He said: ﴿any favor [that] is recompensed﴾, meaning [it is] of the kind whose reward is due on its account.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 92, verse 20:

When he (al-Biqa'i) had negated that he intended by this a reciprocal favour, he said, clarifying his intention by an exceptive construction that is disjunctive (istithna' munqati'): ﴿Except﴾, meaning: rather, he intended by it ﴿seeking﴾, meaning: he sought and aimed at, ﴿the countenance of his Lord﴾ (p-96), and he turned the expression to the attribute of excellence (ihsan), as an indication of describing him with gratitude (shukr), so he said: ﴿the countenance of his Lord﴾, who brought him into existence, nurtured him, and dealt graciously with him, to the degree that he saw no grace except from Him, and nothing was with him except that it was from His bounty, ﴿the Most High﴾, meaning: absolutely, so He is higher than everything. Thus it is not possible that anyone should give from himself something that would constitute a reciprocal favour to Him. He expressed the disjunctive exception with the particle of the connected exception, to indicate that the seeking mentioned is, as it were, a blessing from the One who gave him the wealth, because the seeking, which is the pursuit of God's pleasure, was the cause of that giving, through the utmost encouragement. The matter has come, through this graceful phrasing and elegant indication, together with what it points to of encouragement and what it imparts of endearment, to the meaning: there is no favour upon him to anyone in this except God. He expressed it with "countenance" to indicate that his intention is the highest of intentions, so he has no regard except for the Essence of Him, glorified and exalted, which he expressed by "countenance," because it is the most noble of essences, and by looking at it life, desire and awe are attained, not by seeking anything of this world or the next.

[p. 97] When this was a station above which there is no station, Allah the Exalted said, after His promise of deliverance from the Fire: ﴿And He will surely be pleased.﴾ That is, through the granting of the highest Garden and increase, with a promise that admits no breach, after humiliation in this life, which is a good life. This is indicated by the particle of deferral (*sawfa*, the particle that marks the future). It is no wonder that this promise is of this exalted kind, because the verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, when he bought Bilal, may Allah be pleased with him, along with a group of weak Muslims whom the polytheists were harming, and he freed them. Thus Allah made clear that he was disposed to purify his soul, and so he was the one who succeeds, as mentioned in Surat al-Shams. He was also sincere in giving to the weak among the orphans and the needy, and in freeing the weak in every circumstance, as mentioned in Surat al-Balad.

Al-Baghawi, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him, related from al-Zubayr [i.e., Ibn Bakkar] that he said: Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, used to buy the weak and free them. His father said to him: "My son, if you are going to buy, buy those who will protect your back." He said: "I want only the protection of Allah." He also said: He freed Bilal, Umm 'Umays and Zahra. Her eyesight was afflicted when he freed her, and the Quraysh said: "Only al-Lat and al-'Uzza took away her sight." She said: "They lie, by the House of Allah! al-Lat and al-'Uzza neither harm nor benefit." So Allah restored her sight. He also freed al-Nahdiyya and her daughter, and the slave girl of the Banu al-Mu'ammil. He said: He bought Bilal from Umayya ibn Khalaf, to rescue him from the torment he was suffering, when [Umayya] would bind his hands and feet at the time of the midday heat, throw him naked onto the scorching sand, and beat him. Whenever he struck him, [Bilal] would cry out and call: "One! One!" and [Umayya] would beat him more. [Abu Bakr] bought him in exchange for a slave who belonged to Abu Bakr, a man who was the owner of ten thousand dinars, along with boys, girls, livestock, and who was a polytheist. When he bought Bilal with him and freed him, the polytheists said: "He did this for Bilal only because of a favour Bilal had done for him." So Allah revealed this [verse] to refute them.

Among the most wonderful features is that this surah is followed by Surat al-Duha, which concerns the Prophet ﷺ and contains ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be pleased.﴾ [al-Duha: 5]. This indicates that [Abu Bakr] is the closest of his community to the station of the Prophet ﷺ, apart from 'Isa ﷺ, because he is the most God-fearing after the prophets, without qualification. It also indicates that his caliphate is true, beyond any doubt, because it is among the things the Prophet ﷺ was promised, that it would please him, and that nothing else would please him in the same way. Just as it pleased him, [the Prophet's] appointment of him to lead the prayer, and no one else pleased him when he forbade that; rather, he rebuked [others] when he heard their recitation, and said: "Allah and the believers refuse anyone but Abu Bakr." The end of this surah returns to its beginning, in that the striving of this Siddiq is entirely opposed to the striving of that most wretched one [i.e., Abu Lahab or Umayya; the text refers to "al-Ashqa"]. Some have said: [p. 99] the intended "most wretched one" is Abu Jahl. Also, this concluding part indicates that whoever purifies his soul and makes it grow by being illuminated with inner light, by the illumination that disperses the darkness of night, by the radiance of the Resurrection and other kinds of good, will be pleased by physical light after death. And Allah is the One who grants success in what is right.
